PIE word

First attested in 1954. Early Norwegian use is attested in the hyphenated spelling 3-D; the solid spelling 3D is attested by 1955.
Internationalism, interpreted in Norwegian as an abbreviation of tre (“three”) dimensjoner (“dimensions”) or tredimensjonal (“three-dimensional”). The notation became widespread internationally in connection with stereoscopic film in the early 1950s; English 3-D is attested by 1952, and Swedish 3 D by 1953.

1000315.etyen:
Borrowed from Swedish å (“the letter å”). The letter was introduced into official Norwegian orthography in 1917, replacing the traditional Danish–Norwegian digraph ⟨aa⟩.
The character originated as an early modern German typographical innovation and entered Swedish through the printing press, appearing in works including Olaus Petri's catechism and the Swedish New Testament of 1526. Graphically, it developed from ⟨aa⟩, with the second ⟨a⟩ written above the first and gradually reduced to a ring.
The digraph and later the letter represented the development of Old Norse long á /ɑː/, which became

1001339.etyen:
Clipping of Aleksander (“male given name”), also used as a short form of Alexander (“male given name”). The underlying name is Latin Alexander (“male given name”), from Ancient Greek Ἀλέξανδρος (Aléxandros), traditionally analysed as ἀλέξω (aléxō, “to ward off, defend”) and ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”), genitive ἀνδρός (andrós), hence “defender of men” or “protector of men”.
First attested in the 15th century in Norway.
Compare Danish Sander, Swedish Sander, Dutch Sander and Estonian Sander (“male given name”).

1001595.etyen: Borrowed from Middle Low German feil, fēl, which is borrowed from Old French faille, which is derived from Latin fallō. Cognate with Danish fejl, Swedish fel, German Fehler and English fail. Adverb and adjective derived from the noun.
